```{python}
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (6.6, w_x - 6.2)])
        shade(ax, p, fld, [(-2.0, -SIDELINE), (9.5, -SIDELINE), (9.5, -SIDELINE + 2.0), (-2.0, -SIDELINE + 2.0)],
              style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.12)
        put(ax, p, fld, "sideline\n= help", 1.2, -SIDELINE + 3.6, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        put(ax, p, fld, "taken\naway", 8.3, w_x + 6.4, size=7.0, color=style.INK_2, boxed=False)
        put(ax, p, fld, "inside\nleverage", 1.3, w_x + 4.4, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, boxed=False)
    else:
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (7.2, w_x + 5.5)], ls=(0, (3, 1.5)))
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (7.2, w_x - 5.5)], ls=(0, (3, 1.5)))
        put(ax, p, fld, "in", 7.2, w_x + 6.9, size=7.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, boxed=False, weight="bold")
        put(ax, p, fld, "out", 7.2, w_x - 7.0, size=7.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, boxed=False, weight="bold")
        put(ax, p, fld, "head-up:\nmust guess", 1.4, w_x + 4.4, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, boxed=False)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The defender's position relative to the receiver, inside him, outside him or straight in front, is
called his [leverage](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd), and the quick passing game is
largely a contest of reading it. The point here is about the formation: **where a receiver lines up
decides how many ways he can go, and so how much the defender has to guess.** Slot receivers have
always had two-way gos. Condensed splits give one to the outside receivers too.

The two-way go matters most against man coverage with no help nearby, which is why you'll hear it so
much on third down. If the defense has a safety or a linebacker helping inside, the cornerback can
play outside leverage, give up the inside to his helper and stop guessing. Taking that help away,
by spreading the other defenders out or pulling them toward the run, is the offense's job.

### 3. Crack blocks

The third reason is the run game. A receiver who lines up close to the formation is *already
inside the cornerback* and right next to the defenders he wants to block, close enough to hit them
from the side. A [crack block](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) is a wide
receiver blocking back toward the ball, on a nickel back, linebacker or safety who is watching the
play and not him. It's one of the most effective blocks in football, because the defender is looking
the other way and the receiver gets a running start. From a wide split it takes too long: by the
time the receiver gets back inside, the play is over. From a condensed split he's there in a step or
two.

If that sounds like a cheap shot, the rulebook agrees with you halfway. A crack block is legal, but
only if it's above the waist and not to the head or neck: a receiver who lines up more than two
yards outside the tackle and blocks back toward the ball near the line may not go low, and doing it
costs 15 yards.[^crackback] So the receiver needs to get his eyes and hands on the front of the
defender, chest-high, which is one more reason he wants to start close to him. [Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) has the full rule.

Here's the classic version, a toss (the quarterback pitches the ball underhand to a back who is
already running wide) with the receiver cracking inside and a pulling lineman (one who leaves his
spot at the snap and runs along the line to block somewhere else) replacing him on the cornerback.
Coaches call that pairing *crack-and-replace*. Here the guard pulls; in other versions, like the
one in [Perimeter Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd), the tackle does:

```{python}
#| label: fig-crack-toss
#| fig-cap: "Crack toss from a condensed formation (simulated, BDB-format tracking). 1: X lines up only about eight and a half yards from the ball, outside the nickel back ($) and inside the cornerback (C). 2: the quarterback tosses the ball to the running back (R) heading left; X blocks down (cracks) on the nickel and the left guard pulls around the end. 3: the guard blocks the cornerback, the man X would have blocked from a wide split; H blocks the linebacker W; the left tackle reaches the end, the center cuts off the defensive tackle and the right guard climbs to the middle linebacker. 4: the back turns upfield between X's crack block and the guard's block, with only the deep safety left to beat. The ringed players are the two whose jobs the condensed split makes possible."
crack_off = check_legal(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0.0, "R"),
                                   P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -8.6), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -5.6),
                                   P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 8.6)])
crack_def = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
             D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.2, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
             D("NB", "NB", 4.4, -6.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.2), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.0),
             D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0)]
cp = Play(crack_off, crack_def, los=40, to_go=None)
cp.path("QB", [(-0.6, -0.8)], speed=3.0)
cp.pitch("RB", t=0.35)
cp.run("RB", [(-5.8, -3.5), (-4.4, -7.4), (-1.6, -9.2), (2.6, -8.8), (8.5, -9.0), (13.0, -10.0)],
       absolute=True, speed=7.6)
cp.block("X", pts=[(2.4, 1.0)], speed=6.0)                     # crack down on the nickel
cp.path("NB", [(-0.6, -0.9)], speed=3.0, delay=0.2)            # nickel steps up to force and is met
cp.pull("LG", [(-1.3, -2.4), (-0.1, -7.4), (3.1, -9.6)], speed=7.4)   # guard pulls and "replaces" on the corner
cp.path("LCB", [(-3.1, -1.4)], speed=4.0, delay=0.3)           # corner comes up to force the play
cp.block("H", pts=[(2.4, -0.6), (3.8, 1.6)], speed=5.0)        # H climbs past the end, seals the linebacker
cp.path("WILL", [(-0.8, -1.2)], speed=4.0, delay=0.2)
cp.path("WDE", [(-0.1, -0.3)], speed=2.0)                     # end widens to keep contain
cp.block("LT", pts=[(0.3, -0.7)])                              # reach the end
cp.block("C", pts=[(0.4, -1.0)])                               # cut off the backside-shaded tackle
cp.block("RG", target="MIKE", speed=3.4)                       # climb to the Mike
cp.path("FS", [(-3.5, -2.8)], speed=5.5, delay=0.4)
CRACK_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.4]
CRACK_NOTES = ["Condensed: X starts inside\nthe cornerback",
               "Toss; X cracks the nickel,\nthe guard pulls",
               "The guard 'replaces' X\non the cornerback",
               "The back cuts up between the\nblocks; only the safety is left"]
animated(cp, CRACK_T, CRACK_NOTES, lateral=(-18.5, 9.0), window=(-8.0, 14.5),
         rings=(("X", style.OFFENSE_DARK), ("LG", style.OFFENSE_DARK)))
```

Notice the defender who got blocked. The nickel back was lined up to stop the toss, watching the
ball, and the receiver he was "covering" turned around and hit him from the side. If the nickel
starts watching the receiver instead, the receiver runs past him on a pass. That's the condensed
formation's version of the slot question from earlier in the chapter: a defender who has to worry
about the receiver *and* the run can't do both. The rest of the perimeter run game, including the
jet sweep (a receiver running across the formation at full speed who takes a handoff and keeps
going to the edge), is in [Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

### 4. Everything looks the same

The last reason is the subtlest, and for many coaches the most important. When receivers stand
close to the formation on every play, a run and a pass start from **the same picture**. The
receiver who cracks on a run is lined up exactly where he lines up to run a route on play-action
(faking the handoff, then throwing). The defense can't read the play from the splits. The
condensed formations of the late-2010s Rams and 49ers were built around exactly that: [outside
zone](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) runs (on which the whole line steps sideways
together and the back aims for the edge), crack blocks and [play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
passes, all from one look. The condensed split is also the ideal launch point for a favorite
play-action pass of those offenses: the receiver starts inside the cornerback and just outside the
linebackers, the linebackers step up to stop the fake run, and he crosses the field behind them.
A linebacker or safety who guessed "run" because the receivers were tight was guessing wrong half
the time.

Two more things come with the tight picture. A receiver eight yards from the ball can [motion](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)
across the formation in about a second, so condensed splits and pre-snap motion go naturally together. And the more often the offense lines up this way, the less
any single snap gives away.

### What condensed gives up

Nothing in football is free, and condensing has two clear costs.

**It brings the defense in too.** Defenders line up on receivers, so when the receivers move in,
the defenders move in, and the box can get *more* crowded, not less. The spread's first benefit,
thinning the box, runs backward. Condensed offenses accept that because the receivers now block
those extra defenders, but a condensed formation against a defense that plays it well can feel
very crowded.

**It gives up horizontal stretch.** A spread formation makes defenders cover sideline to sideline; a
condensed one lets them stay closer together, so one defender can sometimes cover two receivers,
and quick throws to the outside, like screens to a receiver near the sideline, have less room. The
[horizontal stretch](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), making defenders cover
too much width, is one of the passing game's basic weapons, and condensing trades some of it for
the other advantages.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Condensed formations exist because the spread taught defenses to play wide.** Once defenses
learned to spread out and play the receivers from the inside, using the sideline as help, the open
space moved: it was now *outside* the receivers and in the [run
fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) near the ball (each
run defender's assigned gap, which a block from an unexpected angle can wipe out). Condensing puts
the receivers where the new space is, and where they can block the defenders who are watching the
ball. It trades width for angles. It's the same idea as the spread, making the defense defend
space it would rather not, aimed at a different patch of grass.
:::

## Specialty looks

Three more formations deserve names, not because you'll see them every drive but because when you
do see them, they're asking a specific question, and you can answer it before the snap.

### Wildcat: a direct snap to someone else

In the [**wildcat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wildcat), the ball is snapped directly to a
running back (or a receiver, or a tight end) standing where the shotgun quarterback would be, while
the real quarterback lines up as a receiver or leaves the field. Usually another back or receiver
runs in motion across the formation at the snap, so the player who takes the snap can hand it to
him, fake to him, or keep it himself.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wildcat
#| fig-cap: "A typical wildcat. The running back (R) stands in the shotgun spot and takes the snap; the quarterback (Q) is split out on the left as a receiver, and the nickel back ($) has gone out with him. A second back (F) runs in motion from the right (dashed) and crosses in front of R at the snap. R either hands it to him on a sweep to the left (give) or keeps it and runs off tackle to the right behind the pulling left guard (keep), a power play. Because the quarterback has drawn a defender out of the box, the offense has one more blocker or runner near the ball than a normal handoff would give it. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, W, M and S = the Will, Mike and Sam (strongside) linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS = free safety."
wc = check_legal(line5() + [P("RB", "RB", GUN, 0, "R"), P("QB", "QB", OFF_BALL, -11.8, "Q"),
                            P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                            P("F", "RB", OFF_BALL, 9.0, "F"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.5)])
wd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 7.4), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -11.8, "$"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0)]
wp = Play(wc, wd, los=40, to_go=None)
wp.motion("F", to=(-2.6, 1.2))
wp.run("F", [(-2.2, -3.0), (-0.6, -9.0), (3.2, -13.0), (8.5, -14.5)], absolute=True)
wp.pull("LG", [(-1.5, 1.4), (-1.5, 4.0), (1.3, 4.9)])          # the power puller leads up through the hole
wp.highlight("RB", color=RB_RING)
wp.highlight("F", color=RB_RING)
wp.highlight("QB", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = wp.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-8.0, 14.5), title=False)
ax = plt.gca()
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
branch(ax, wp, fld, [(GUN, 0.0), (-3.4, 2.6), (-1.8, 4.0), (6.2, 4.0)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4)
put(ax, wp, fld, "keep", 7.2, 4.0, size=7.4, boxed=False, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
put(ax, wp, fld, "give", 9.6, -14.5, size=7.4, boxed=False, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
put(ax, wp, fld, "QB split\nout wide", -4.6, -11.8, size=7.2)
plt.show()
```

Why snap to a running back? Think about a normal handoff. The quarterback takes the snap, hands the
ball off, and then does nothing useful for the run: he's one of the offense's eleven players, but
he isn't blocking anybody. The defense, meanwhile, has all eleven of its players available to
tackle. In the wildcat, the player who takes the snap is himself a running threat. And the
quarterback, now split out wide, still needs a defender on him, because he is still an eligible
receiver: leave him alone and the offense can throw to him, or toss him the ball back for a pass of
his own. So the offense has one more player who matters to the run and the defense has one fewer to
stop it. The motion man adds a second runner, so the defense can't key on one ball carrier.

The wildcat's ancestor is the [single wing](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd),
the direct-snap formation that ruled football before the [T-formation](02-03-classic-formations.qmd). Its modern NFL moment came in
2008, when the Miami Dolphins used it to stun the New England Patriots (the story is in the film
room below), and for a season or two teams all over the league copied it. Then it faded, for a reason worth
remembering: the player taking the snap usually couldn't throw. Once defenses stopped respecting
the pass, they put an extra player in the box, and the wildcat's one-player advantage disappeared.
It survives today in short bursts, as a short-yardage or goal-line package, or built around a
player who really can both run and throw. In Next Gen Stats' formation labels it never reached even
one play in a hundred in any season from 2016 to 2022.[^wildcat-rate]

### Unbalanced line: tackle over

An [**unbalanced line**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-unbalanced-line) puts more offensive
linemen on one side of the center than the other. The common way, [**tackle
over**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-over), moves one tackle to line up next to the other
one, so one side has three linemen outside the center and the other side has only a guard.

```{python}
#| label: fig-unbalanced
#| fig-cap: "Balanced and unbalanced, against the same defensive front. Left: a normal line, two linemen on each side of the center, with the tight end (Y, gold ring) on the right. Counting the right side of the center, three blockers (the right guard, the right tackle and Y) face four defenders (the tackle T, the end E and the linebackers M and S). Right: tackle over. The left tackle (dark ring) lines up outside the right tackle, so the right side has three linemen plus the tight end, and the left side has only the guard. X lines up on the line on the left to keep seven on the line; he is now the left end. If the defense doesn't shift its front, the right side is now four blockers against four defenders: everyone has a man, and the back runs behind them. Q = quarterback, R = running back; linemen unlettered; S = Sam linebacker; C = cornerbacks; $ = nickel back."
def unbal(over):
    q, rb = P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R")
    if over:
        ol = [Player("LG", "LG", "off", LINE_D, -OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0, label=""),
              Player("RG", "RG", "off", LINE_D, OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("RT", "RT", "off", LINE_D, 2 * OL_SPLIT, label=""),
              Player("LT", "LT", "off", LINE_D, 3 * OL_SPLIT, label="")]
        skill = [q, rb, P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4 * OL_SPLIT + 1.0), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -10.0),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -6.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]
    else:
        ol = line5()
        skill = [q, rb, P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.0)]
    return check_legal(ol + skill)


ud = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 7.2), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -11.0), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -7.0, "$"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 12.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0)]
LAT, WIN = (-16, 16), (-8.5, 13.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, over, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "Balanced"), (axes[0, 1], True, "Tackle over")]:
    p = Play(unbal(over), ud, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
    if over:
        p.highlight("LT", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    put(ax, p, fld, "2 linemen | 2 linemen" if not over else "1 lineman | 3 linemen", -4.4, 0.0,
        size=7.0, color=style.INK_2)
    put(ax, p, fld, ("right side:\n4 blockers vs 4" if over else "right side:\n3 blockers vs 4"), 9.8, 8.6,
        size=7.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK if over else style.INK, weight="bold" if over else "normal")
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The point is arithmetic. A defense lines up its front by counting blockers on each side of the
center. If one side suddenly has an extra lineman and the defense doesn't notice or doesn't shift,
the offense has a blocker for every defender on that side, and it runs there. The defense's simplest
answer is to declare the extra-lineman side its strong side and slide its whole front a gap over,
which works if everyone sees it in time, and can open a hole somewhere else or leave a pass-rusher
out of position if they don't.

Moving the left tackle isn't the only way to get there. An offense can also bring in a sixth
offensive lineman to stand next to a tackle, which gives the same extra blocker without
weakening the other side of the line.

Two rules keep the look honest. Linemen wear numbers 50 to 79 and are ineligible, so a tackle who
moves to the end of the line is still just a blocker, which is why a tight end usually lines up
outside him if the offense wants to threaten a pass that way. And the line still needs seven men, so
the side left with only a guard needs a receiver on the line at its end, like X in the picture. (A
lineman can become eligible by [reporting to the referee](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd),
a different trick.)

### Swinging gate: make the defense follow

The [**swinging gate**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-swinging-gate) is a trick alignment you'll
see mostly on extra points and two-point tries. The snapper stays over the ball, with the holder
behind him, and most of the other linemen line up in a group far out to one side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swinging-gate
#| fig-cap: "A swinging gate on an extra-point try. Only the snapper (the lone lineman at the ball) is over the ball, with the holder (P, usually the punter) and kicker (K) behind him. Four linemen and a tight end stand on the line far to the right, with a second tight end (U) and a receiver (Z) behind them: the 'gate,' seven players in all. A receiver (X) on the line on the far left gives the formation its seventh man on the line, so it's legal. Here the defense has sent only four players out to the gate (two cornerbacks, C, and two safeties, FS and SS), so the gate's six blockers can take all four while Z carries the ball; if more defenders follow, the offense shifts back into its normal kicking formation (the gate 'swings shut'). Defense at the ball: E = ends, T = tackles, LB = linebackers."
gate_off = check_legal([
    P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -13.0), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label=""),
    Player("G1", "LG", "off", LINE_D, 9.6, label=""), Player("G2", "LT", "off", LINE_D, 11.2, label=""),
    Player("G3", "RG", "off", LINE_D, 12.8, label=""), Player("G4", "RT", "off", LINE_D, 14.4, label=""),
    P("T2", "TE", LINE_D, 16.2, "Y"),
    P("HOLD", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "P"), Player("K", "K", "off", -9.5, -1.6, label="K"),
    P("T1", "TE", -2.2, 11.2, "U"), P("W1", "WR", -2.2, 14.4, "Z")])
gate_def = [D("D1", "DE", 1.0, -3.0, "E"), D("D2", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "T"), D("D3", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "T"),
            D("D4", "DE", 1.0, 3.0, "E"), D("D5", "LB", 1.0, -5.0, "LB"), D("D6", "LB", 1.0, 5.0, "LB"),
            D("D7", "CB", 4.5, -13.0, "C"), D("D8", "CB", 4.0, 10.6, "C"), D("D9", "SS", 5.5, 13.2, "SS"),
            D("D10", "CB", 4.0, 16.0, "C"), D("D11", "FS", 8.0, 12.0, "FS")]
gp = Play(gate_off, gate_def, los=95, to_go=None)
fld = gp.draw(lateral=(-16.5, 21.0), window=(-11.5, 10.0), title=False)
ax = plt.gca()
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
shade(ax, gp, fld, [(-3.4, 8.4), (2.4, 8.4), (2.4, 17.6), (-3.4, 17.6)], style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.08, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
put(ax, gp, fld, "the 'gate': 5 on the line,\n2 behind (7 players)", -5.4, 13.0, size=7.2)
put(ax, gp, fld, "4 defenders\nfollowed", 7.8, 18.0, size=7.2, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

The gate asks the defense a yes-or-no question. If the defense lines up to block the kick and
ignores the group out wide, the offense snaps the ball to the holder, who throws to or pitches to the
gate, where there are more offensive players than defenders: in the picture, six blockers for four
defenders, and a seventh man to carry the ball. If the defense sends people out to
cover the gate, the gate "swings shut": the linemen run back to their normal spots and the team kicks,
or the offense uses the defense's confusion to run a play from the normal formation. Either way the
defense has to recognize it, count it, and adjust in a few seconds, which is exactly the kind of
pressure every formation in this chapter is designed to create.[^pat]

## Where spread formations came from

The full story belongs to Part 11, but three sentences explain why the NFL looks the way it does.
Spreading receivers out is almost as old as the forward pass: Dutch Meyer's TCU teams of the 1930s
and 1940s used what he called the "spread formation," and from the late 1950s on, the run and shoot
and later the [Air Raid](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd) turned
the idea into whole offenses, mostly in high school and college.[^history] The NFL came to it slowly,
then all at once, as a generation of quarterbacks and receivers arrived having played nearly every
snap in the shotgun with three or four receivers out, and as offenses like the 2007 Patriots (see the
film room) showed what it could do; by the late 2010s the shotgun 11-personnel spread was the league's
default, and the condensed formation was the next move in the same back-and-forth. [The College
Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) and [The Modern
Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd) tell it in full.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England Patriots 2007"}
The 2007 Patriots went 16–0 in the regular season and scored 589 points, at the time an NFL
record. Tom Brady threw 50 touchdown passes (also a record then), Randy Moss caught 23 of them (a
single-season record), and Wes Welker caught 112 passes.[^pats07] The offense, coordinated by Josh
McDaniels, lived in spread formations: by the play-by-play data's shotgun flag, the Patriots were
in the shotgun on about half their plays, more than any other team and nearly twice the league rate
of about 27%.

The spread was built around two very different receivers, and it shows the two halves of this
chapter. **Moss** was the deep threat outside, exactly the kind of receiver a 3x1 leaves on the
island: a defense that rotated its safety away from him left him one-on-one with a cornerback, and
a defense that kept a safety over him was short-handed everywhere else. **Welker** worked from the
slot, where he had a two-way go on most snaps and could break inside or outside depending on how the
defender played him.[^pats07-roles]

**What to notice:** when an offense puts one receiver alone on one side and three on the other, find
the safeties. Where they go before the snap tells you which bet the defense is making, and which
receiver the quarterback will look at first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
Sean McVay's 2018 Rams went 13–3 and reached Super Bowl LIII, and as [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
showed, they used 11 personnel on about 93% of their plays. With the personnel never changing, the
variety had to come from formation and motion, and the Rams' signature was the **condensed
formation**: receivers lined up close to the formation, so tight that about 60% of the Rams'
formations were less than 20 yards wide at the snap, against 37% for the next-tightest team. (For
scale: a 2x2 with both outside receivers on the numbers and the ball in the middle is about 25 to
30 yards wide from one outside receiver to the other.)

The tight splits made the run game and the passing game look alike. On outside zone runs, the
receivers were close enough to block the linebackers and safeties at the edge; on play-action and
bootlegs, the same receivers released into routes from the same spots, and defenders who had been hit
by those receivers on the previous run had to guess.[^rams18]

**What to notice:** before the snap, measure the outside receiver against the numbers painted on the
field. If he's well inside them, look for a crack block on a run or an outside-breaking route on a pass,
and watch the cornerback: if he widens to protect the outside, the inside is open.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins 2008, the Wildcat"}
On September 21, 2008, the Miami Dolphins, who had gone 1–15 the year before, traveled to New
England and beat the Patriots 38–13. Running back Ronnie Brown took direct snaps in a formation the
Dolphins called the Wildcat and scored four rushing touchdowns, and threw a touchdown pass from it as
well. Miami stacked two of this chapter's tricks: the Wildcat line was unbalanced, and the handful of
plays (a power, a counter, a sweep to Ricky Williams coming across in motion, a reverse and a couple
of passes) all started from the same picture. The loss ended New England's 21-game regular-season winning streak, and Miami went on to win the
AFC East at 11–5.[^dolphins08]

The idea came to Miami through quarterbacks coach David Lee, who had run a version of it at the
University of Arkansas with Darren McFadden. The name has a longer and disputed history: several high
school and college coaches ran direct-snap formations under the same name in the late 1990s and 2000s,
and all of them were rediscovering the single wing.[^wildcat-origin]

**What to notice:** when a running back walks up to the shotgun spot and the quarterback jogs out wide,
count the box. The wildcat's edge is one extra runner; if the defense has one extra defender inside,
it has taken that edge away, and the offense's best play may be to shift back out of it.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: formation and leverage"}
- **Name the formation.** As the offense breaks the huddle, count receivers on each side, from the
  sideline in: 2x2, 3x1, empty (3x2), or a variation (bunch, stack, nub, quads). Is anybody beside the
  quarterback?
- **Find the strength.** Which side has more receivers? Is the tight end on the same side or the other
  one (a nub)? A split strength means the defense has to pick one.
- **Check the splits.** Use the painted numbers as your ruler. An outside receiver on or outside the
  numbers is a normal or wide split; one clearly inside the numbers (a high camera shows it best) is
  condensed, and one within a few yards of the tackle or tight end is tight. Condensed splits mean
  crack blocks, outside-breaking routes, play-action crossers and rubs; wide splits mean the offense
  wants the defense spread thin.
- **Count each side, three steps.** Receivers on that side; underneath defenders outside the box on
  that side (an apex defender counts); then the deep safety as "+ safety." More receivers than
  underneath defenders is a quick throw waiting to happen; a lone receiver with no safety on his side
  is on an island.
- **Count the box.** Did the spread pull defenders out? Six or fewer in the box against a spread
  formation is an invitation to run.
- **Look for specialty clues.** The quarterback split out wide: wildcat. Three linemen on one side of
  the center: unbalanced. Linemen standing far out on an extra point: swinging gate.
- **Log it.** Add a "formation" column to your [prediction
  log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) beside personnel: for example "11, 3x1
  right, condensed." After a half, check how often empty meant pass.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: count the sides"}
Second-and-6 at midfield. The offense is in 11 personnel and lines up like this; the defense is in
nickel with two deep safeties.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-count
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M and W = linebackers, $ = nickel back, C = cornerbacks, FS and SS = safeties (both about 12 yards deep). Shaded rectangle = the box. Offense: X, H and Z are wide receivers, Y the tight end (gold ring), R the running back (aqua ring), Q the quarterback. The thick gold line across the field, in all three drills, is the line to gain."
dd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -1.2), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.6),
      D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.5), D("NB", "NB", 4.6, 11.6, "$"),
      D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 9.5)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(form("3x1"), dd, los=60, to_go=6))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False, width_in=5.2)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
shade_box(plt.gca(), q, fld)
plt.show()
```

**Name the formation and number the receivers. Where does the offense have more receivers than
defenders, and what's the likely play?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**3x1 (trips right).** On the right, Z is #1, H is #2 and the tight end Y is #3; on the left, X is #1.
The back beside the quarterback isn't numbered.

**Count the right side, three steps:** three receivers; two underneath defenders outside the box
(the cornerback on Z and the nickel on H); and the safety, twelve yards deep, as "+ safety." The
linebacker W is inside the box, so he doesn't count, and the third receiver, Y, has nobody within
about seven yards. That's three against two underneath.

**The likely play:** a quick throw to the trips side, to Y or on a screen to the three-receiver side,
before the defense can bring the safety down or widen W. If W walks out before the snap, the box drops
to five and the run looks better: that's the slot question from earlier in the chapter. Either way,
the defense's alignment has handed the offense a numbers advantage, and good offenses check to it.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: empty with a running quarterback"}
Third-and-4 at the opponent's 40. The offense has a quarterback who's one of the league's best
runners. It goes empty, and the defense matches with six defensive backs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-empty
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2. Empty 3x2 against a dime defense (six defensive backs). Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M = linebacker, C = cornerbacks, $ = nickel, D = dime back, FS and SS = safeties. Shaded rectangle = the box."
ed = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -1.6, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 1.6, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.0),
      D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.0, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 5.5, 7.6, "D"),
      D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 10.8), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -3.0)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(form("empty"), ed, los=70, to_go=4))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False, width_in=5.2)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
shade_box(plt.gca(), q, fld)
plt.show()
```

**Is this a pass? What does the defense's alignment invite, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Probably a pass, but watch for a quarterback run.** League-wide, empty is nearly always a
dropback, and third-and-4 is a passing down. That's the default.

**What the alignment invites:** count the box. Four linemen and one linebacker: **five** defenders
inside, against **five** offensive linemen. Every box defender has a blocker. The other six defenders
are spread out over the five receivers: the strong safety has walked up over the tight end, and the
free safety is alone, thirteen yards deep. If the quarterback is a real running threat, a quarterback
draw (he drops back as if to pass, then runs up the middle) has the numbers: every box defender
blocked, and the quarterback against defensive backs who are backing up to cover receivers. If the
coverage is man, it's even better, because the man defenders turn and run with their receivers,
their backs to the quarterback. That's the arithmetic behind the Bills' empty runs with Josh Allen.

**The defense's dilemma:** to take the draw away it needs a sixth defender in the box, and the only
place to get one is from coverage over five receivers. That's what empty is for.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: everybody's tight"}
First-and-10 at the offense's own 35. The offense lines up in 11 personnel with the quarterback under
center and the receivers squeezed in.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-condensed
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3. A condensed 2x2 with the ball in the middle of the field: X and Z about eight and a half yards from the ball, H and the tight end Y inside them, the quarterback (Q) under center and the back (R) behind him. The defense has lined up as if the receivers were still wide: both cornerbacks (C) are a couple of yards *inside* the receivers they cover, with a nickel back ($), two linebackers (W, M) and two deep safeties (FS, SS)."
cd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("NB", "NB", 4.2, -4.9, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -6.6), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 6.6),
      D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.5), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.5)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(crack_off, cd, los=45, to_go=10))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-SIDELINE, SIDELINE), window=(-8.0, 13.0), title=False, width_in=6.5)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()
```

**Where is the open grass, and what kinds of play does this formation set up? What would you expect
the cornerbacks to do about it, and what does that set up?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The open grass is outside the receivers:** about 18 yards between each outside receiver and his
sideline, and the cornerbacks, lined up *inside* them, aren't protecting any of it.

**What it sets up right now:**

1. **Outside-breaking routes:** an [out](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) (straight up, then a sharp cut to the sideline), a corner
   (up, then angling toward the back corner of the end zone) or a fade (a deep throw toward the
   sideline). With the cornerback inside him, the receiver doesn't even need his two-way go; he has
   a one-way go to the side the defender isn't protecting.
2. **Play-action.** It's first down, the quarterback is under center and the receivers are tight:
   the defense has to respect the run. A fake handoff pulls the linebackers forward, and the receivers
   can release behind them or outside the cornerbacks.

**What the corners should do:** widen and play outside leverage, protecting the grass. (Good
defenses do this before the offense can punish them; the drill shows a defense that hasn't.) But
look at what that creates. With the corners outside the receivers, X and Z are now *outside the
nickel and the linebackers and inside the cornerbacks*, exactly the picture the crack toss started
from. X can crack down on the nickel while a pulling lineman takes the cornerback. And with the
corners guarding the outside, the inside opens for slants and digs (a dig is a route that goes
straight up the field, then cuts flat across it). The defense can take away one thing; the formation
has set up the other.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **A formation is where the players stand, and a spread formation puts the pass-catchers across the
  width of the field.** It makes the defense defend all 53⅓ yards, thins the box and forces defenders to
  show where they're going. Personnel doesn't change; one grouping can line up a dozen ways.
- **Count receivers from the sideline in, side by side: #1, #2, #3.** That count names the formation
  (2x2, 3x1, empty 3x2, quads 4x1) and sets the defense's coverage rules. Then count each side in three
  steps (receivers, underneath defenders outside the box, the deep safety) to see where the offense
  has the numbers.
- **Every spread formation asks the defense a question it can't answer both ways.** Cover the slot or
  stay in the box; help the trips side or the lone receiver; match an empty set with defensive backs or
  keep a sixth man inside. The offense does whatever the defense didn't.
- **Clusters and lopsided formations have specific jobs.** Bunch and stack beat man coverage and press
  with traffic and free releases; nub splits the formation's strength; quads asks a question most
  defenses haven't practiced. Empty shows the quarterback everything but is more than 94% pass.
- **Count and width are two separate dials.** 2x2, 3x1 and empty describe the count; spread and
  condensed describe the width. Condensed splits are the modern counter-move: pulling receivers in
  gives them room outside, a two-way go, angles for crack blocks and a way to make runs and passes look
  alike, at the cost of some width and a more crowded box. It differs from the old tight formations
  because the bodies are wide receivers, so the defense has to stay small.
- **Specialty looks (wildcat, unbalanced, swinging gate) are arithmetic tricks.** Each one adds a blocker
  or a runner somewhere the defense hasn't counted. Count the defense's answer before the snap.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (measure receiver splits from real tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
print(plays["receiverAlignment"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))   # 2x2, 3x1, 3x2 ...

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
snap = trk[trk["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
ball = snap[snap["displayName"] == "football"][["gameId", "playId", "y"]].rename(columns={"y": "ball_y"})
wr = snap.merge(players, on="nflId").query("position == 'WR'").merge(ball, on=["gameId", "playId"])
wr["split"] = (wr["y"] - wr["ball_y"]).abs()                 # yards from the ball, across the field
widest = wr.groupby(["gameId", "playId", "club"])["split"].max()
print(widest.groupby("club").median().sort_values())        # the most condensed offenses come first
```
:::

[^condensed]: Domonique Foxworth, "Yes, Sean McVay is an offensive genius," Andscape, Jan. 29, 2019 (Rams' condensed formations): <https://andscape.com/features/rams-coach-sean-mcvay-is-an-offensive-genius>; Zach Barnett, "How Kyle Shanahan has mastered the play-calling trend that's sweeping the NFL," FootballScoop, Feb. 6, 2024, summarizing a *Wall Street Journal* analysis of Next Gen Stats data (condensed about 11% of plays in 2016; tight splits overtook the spread in 2023; the 49ers' formations the narrowest in the league, about 19.9 yards end to end): <https://footballscoop.com/news/how-kyle-shanahan-has-mastered-the-play-calling-trend-thats-sweeping-the-nfl>.

[^empty-pers]: Course calculation from nflverse data: 2025 regular-season runs and passes with no offensive player in the backfield (FTN charting), joined to the participation file's personnel. 11 personnel made up 71.7% of empty snaps, 12 personnel 14.9%, and every other grouping 3% or less.

[^empty-data]: Course calculation from nflverse data (`load_pbp`, `load_participation`, `load_ftn_charting`), regular-season plays with `play_type` of pass or run and a recorded down. Empty through 2022 is the Next Gen Stats `offense_formation` label "EMPTY" (the fewer than 1% of plays with no formation label are left out); from 2022 it is FTN's `n_offense_backfield` equal to zero. In 2022, the one season both sources cover, they agree at 8.1%. A pass is any dropback, including sacks and scrambles. Data dictionaries: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_participation.html> and <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html>.

[^opi]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 5 (pass interference): pass interference is an act more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage that significantly hinders an eligible player's opportunity to catch the ball; for the offense the restrictions run from the snap until the ball is touched, and "blocking downfield by an offensive player prior to the ball being touched" (the pick play) is the first listed example of offensive pass interference: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^pat]: The NFL moved the extra-point kick back to a snap from the 15-yard line in May 2015 (a 30–2 owners' vote); two-point tries stayed at the 2. Gregg Rosenthal, "NFL moves extra point to 15-yard line for 2015 season," NFL.com, May 19, 2015: <https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-moves-extra-point-to-15-yard-line-for-2015-season-0ap3000000493347>. Both are unchanged for 2026.

[^history]: Meyer (TCU head coach 1934–1952) and his book *Spread Formation Football* (1952): "Dutch Meyer," Wikipedia, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Meyer>, and "Spread offense," <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spread_offense>. The run and shoot grew from Glenn "Tiger" Ellison's 1958 "Lonesome Polecat" formation at Middletown (Ohio) High School, was refined by Darrel "Mouse" Davis at Portland State in the 1970s and was the base offense of the Oilers, Lions and Falcons by the early 1990s: Dusty Evely, "Tiger Ellison and the Run and Shoot," summarizing Ellison's *Run and Shoot Football: Offense of the Future*: <https://dustyevely.substack.com/p/tiger-ellison-and-the-run-and-shoot>; "Run and shoot offense," Wikipedia, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_and_shoot_offense>. Hal Mumme and Mike Leach built the Air Raid at Iowa Wesleyan (1989–1991), Valdosta State (1992–1996) and Kentucky (1997–1998): "Mike Leach (American football coach)," Wikipedia, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Leach_(American_football_coach)>. For the wider story: Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015).

[^pats07]: Pro Football Reference, 2007 New England Patriots: <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nwe/2007.htm> (16–0; 589 points; Brady 50 TD passes; Moss 23 TD receptions; Welker 112 receptions). The 2013 Denver Broncos later scored 606 points, and Peyton Manning threw 55 touchdown passes the same season. The Patriots lost Super Bowl XLII to the New York Giants, 17–14. Shotgun shares are a course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`shotgun` flag, 2007 regular-season runs and passes): New England 50.3%, first in the league; league 26.9%.

[^pats07-roles]: Welker's slot role and the three- and four-receiver sets: "The Near-Perfect Football Team," The Ringer, Aug. 7, 2017: <https://www.theringer.com/nfl/2017/8/7/16107814/2007-new-england-patriots-tom-brady-randy-moss-wes-welker>, which also describes the safety dilemma Moss created. How often Moss lined up alone on one side isn't recorded in the public data, so the text describes the dilemma rather than a frequency.

[^rams18]: Pro Football Reference, 2018 Los Angeles Rams: <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/ram/2018.htm> (13–3; lost Super Bowl LIII to New England, 13–3). The 11-personnel share is a course calculation from nflverse participation data (see [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)). Formation widths (ESPN Analytics and Next Gen Stats, through the 2018 season) and the condensed sets' uses, outside runs, receivers blocking and receivers releasing on bootlegs: Domonique Foxworth, "Yes, Sean McVay is an offensive genius," Andscape, Jan. 29, 2019: <https://andscape.com/features/rams-coach-sean-mcvay-is-an-offensive-genius>.

[^dolphins08]: Pro Football Reference box score, Miami 38, New England 13 (Sept. 21, 2008): <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200809210nwe.htm>. Brown's four rushing touchdowns and touchdown pass (19 yards to Anthony Fasano), the end of New England's 21-game regular-season winning streak, Miami's 1–15 2007 and 11–5 AFC East title in 2008, and David Lee's Arkansas version with Darren McFadden and Felix Jones: ESPN, "Wildcat strike: How 2008 Dolphins shocked Patriots and the NFL": <https://www.espn.com/blog/miami-dolphins/post/_/id/28295/wildcat-strike-how-2008-dolphins-shocked-patriots-and-the-nfl>; Pro Football Hall of Fame, "Wildcat immortalized": <https://www.profootballhof.com/news/wildcat-immortalized>.

[^wildcat-origin]: "Wildcat formation," Wikipedia: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildcat_formation>. The *Wall Street Journal* credited Hugh Wyatt, whose La Center (Washington) High School Wildcats ran a direct-snap version from 1997 and who described it in *Scholastic Coach* in 1998, with the name; Bill Snyder's Kansas State Wildcats are also often cited as its namesake; Arkansas called its version the "Wild Hog." Lee's role in bringing it to Miami: the ESPN piece in the note above.

[^bills]: Course calculation from nflverse data. Empty share: Next Gen Stats formation labels (2019–2022) and FTN backfield counts (2023–2025), regular-season runs and passes: Buffalo 10.0% of plays over 2019–2025, league 8.3%. Designed runs (runs that weren't scrambles) as a share of empty snaps in 2023: Buffalo 12.7% (14 of 110, 13 by Allen), the rest of the league 5.3% (5.6% with Buffalo included). Allen's listed height and weight: <https://www.buffalobills.com/team/players-roster/josh-allen/>.

[^chiefs]: Barry Petchesky, Super Bowl LVII film breakdown, Defector, Feb. 13, 2023, on Kansas City's stacked receivers in Super Bowl LVII and Andy Reid's comment that the winning design worked against man coverage: <https://defector.com/chiefs-super-bowl-confuse-the-eagles-defense-with-this-one-weird-trick>.

[^crackback]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 12, Section 2, Article 6 ("crackback" block): a player who lines up more than two yards outside the tackle, or is in motion or moves that wide, and blocks back toward the spot of the snap within five yards of the line of scrimmage may not contact an opponent below the waist or in the head or neck area; 15 yards: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. The rule and the newer blindside-block ban are covered in [Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

[^empty-2025]: Course calculation from nflverse data: regular-season runs and passes with FTN's `n_offense_backfield` equal to zero, joined to the participation file's `offense_personnel` (11 personnel = one running back or fullback, one tight end, three wide receivers). Empty share of 11-personnel snaps: 10.6% in 2024, 8.6% in 2025; of all other snaps, about 5.4% and 4.7%. 11 personnel itself fell from about 62% to 57% of these plays.

[^no-2x2]: Next Gen Stats' formation labels in the free participation data (2016–2022) say only SHOTGUN, SINGLEBACK, I_FORM, EMPTY and the like, and from 2023 just SHOTGUN, UNDER CENTER and PISTOL; FTN's charting counts players in the backfield but not where the receivers stand. The NFL's Big Data Bowl 2025 files (2022 season, weeks 1–9, on Kaggle with a free login) do have a `receiverAlignment` label ("2x2," "3x1," "3x2" and so on) for every play; starter code is in the "Go deeper" box at the end of the chapter's web edition. We couldn't find a published league-wide count to cite.

[^wildcat-rate]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (Next Gen Stats `offense_formation` label "WILDCAT"), regular-season runs and passes, 2016–2022: between 0.2% and 0.7% of plays each season. The label was dropped from 2023.
